summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach friction as a FORCE between two surfaces that opposes sliding motion, not merely a property of 'rough things'. Central activity: send the SAME object across several surfaces (ice, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper) as a fair test, measure distance travelled, and represent the invisible friction with a force arrow pointing against the motion. Use the Institute of Physics grip/slip framing, connect slip to warming, and confront the 'push runs out' impetus idea plus the 'shiny = slippery' confusion. For grip (static friction), be clear it balances an applied push or a slope's pull — a still object with nothing pushing it has no horizontal friction. Includes consolidation sorting/ordering, an annotated real-world reference, and a two-tier diagnostic.
misconceptions: Friction is a phenomenon or a 'thing', not named/treated as a force (IOP).
Friction only acts when things move (slip) — or the mirror error, only when things are still (grip); both are partial views (IOP).
Friction is always bad/undesirable, ignoring that grip is what lets us walk and brake.
Things stop because the push/force 'runs out', rather than because friction pushes back (impetus link).
Confusing smoothness with shininess ('shiny = slippery'); and comparing rolling resistance with sliding as if they were the same.
Reasoning backwards from effect to cause — 'it took a long time to stop, so the friction must have been small' (IOP tripwire).

activities.title: Same object, different surfaces: a fair-test friction runway
steps: Set up a flat runway (physical track, or a screen simulation of one) and choose one object (e.g. a puck or wooden block) that you will NOT change between runs.
Before each run, predict how far the object will travel and mark your predicted stopping point.

Give the object the same push each time (e.g. release it from the same point on a small launch ramp or pull back a rubber band by the same amount, since hand flicks vary), send it across at least three different surfaces in turn (e.g. ice/very smooth, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper), repeat each run a few times, and keep everything else the same so only the surface changes.
Measure and record how far it travelled on each surface in a data table (surface ↔ distance), and build up a simple bar chart so the pattern becomes visible.
Order the surfaces from 'object travels furthest' to 'stops soonest' and describe the pattern in your own words.
activities.insight: Changing only the surface changes how far the same pushed object travels before it slows to a stop: rougher surfaces produce more friction and stop the object sooner. This is a fair test — keep the object and the push the same, change only the surface.

activities.title: Forces spectacles: drawing the invisible friction arrow
steps: After a run, draw a force arrow on the moving object pointing BACKWARDS, against the direction it is sliding — this represents the friction slowing it.
Compare runs: draw a short arrow for a smooth surface and a longer arrow for a rough surface, matching 'more friction = longer arrow'.
Say out loud which way friction pushes and why the object slows: friction is a force from the surfaces acting against the sliding motion.
Optionally, in a screen simulation, toggle a 'forces spectacles' overlay that shows the opposing arrow growing longer on rougher surfaces, and watch a warming meter glow on the rough, sliding runs.
activities.insight: Friction is a force acting between two surfaces in contact, opposing their sliding. Though invisible, it can be represented by an arrow pointing against the motion; it is larger on rougher surfaces, which is why the object slows and stops sooner.

activities.title: Grip and slip, and the warming you can feel
steps: Rub your hands together quickly and feel them warm up — notice that sliding (slip) between surfaces produces heat.
Discuss grip: push gently on a shoe (or block) resting on a path and notice it does NOT slide until you push hard — static (grip) friction is balancing your push before the object moves.

Sort example situations into grip (prevents sliding: walking without slipping, standing on a slope without sliding, a parked object on a slope held in place, brakes holding) and slip (slows an existing slide: a sledge stopping, a skidding object).
Discuss friction as both helpful (grip lets us walk and lets brakes work) and unhelpful (slows a sledge) so friction is not labelled simply 'bad'.
activities.insight: Friction has two faces. Grip (static friction) can act on a still object WHEN something pushes it or it rests on a slope — it balances that push up to the point the object starts to slide. Slip (sliding friction) slows an object already sliding and warms the surfaces. Friction is both helpful and unhelpful depending on the situation.

activities.title: Shiny is not the same as slippery (predict–observe–explain)
steps: Take two surfaces: crumpled-then-flattened kitchen foil (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card (dull but smooth).
Predict which lets the same block slide further, and say WHY before testing.
Slide the block on each with the same push and observe which surface lets it slide further; in most setups the block grips the crinkled shiny foil more and slides further on the smooth dull card.
Explain what your results suggest mattered (usually roughness, not shininess) and restate that friction is a force from the surfaces opposing motion.
Extra challenge: would a coin slide the same on a shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass? Discuss what really decides it.
activities.insight: Shininess does not determine friction; what matters is the surfaces in contact: mainly how rough or smooth they are, and also what they are made of. 'Shiny = slippery' is a trap.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sort, order, and explain
steps: Order a set of surfaces by how far the object slides on each (furthest → stops soonest).
Sort everyday situations into friction that is helpful (walking, braking) versus unhelpful (slowing a sledge).
Match each surface to a grip or slip description.

Answer the diagnostic: 'I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what about that surface stops it?' Give the mechanism, not just the outcome.
Reason about a still object: if you push gently on a block resting on a table but it does not move, is any friction acting on it? How could you tell (what happens as you push harder)?
activities.insight: A full understanding names friction as a FORCE between the two surfaces, acting opposite the motion and larger on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises that friction can also act on a still object being pushed or on a slope (grip/static friction balancing the push).

checkQuestion: I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving it the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what is it about that surface that stops it?
checkAnswer: It stops sooner on the rough carpet. The rough surface produces more friction — a force between the block and the surface that acts against the block's motion and slows it; the smooth table has less friction so the block slides further.
